c1.function: Cradles the skull and transmits its entire weight into the neck through its two lateral masses, acting as a bony washer that lets the head nod ("yes") at the atlanto-occipital joints.
articulates_with: Occipital condyles of the skull (atlanto-occipital joints)
The axis (C2), via the median atlantoaxial joint with the dens and the two lateral atlantoaxial facet joints
c1.note: Named for the Titan Atlas, who held up the heavens. It is the only vertebra with neither a body nor a true spinous process (it has a posterior tubercle instead) — its centrum separated in development and contributes to the dens of C2. Axial loading, classically diving into shallow water, drives the occipital condyles into its ring and bursts it: a Jefferson fracture.

c2.function: Provides the dens (odontoid process), the vertical peg around which the atlas and the whole head pivot; the atlantoaxial joints supply roughly half of all cervical rotation.
articulates_with: The atlas (C1), via the median atlantoaxial joint and the two lateral atlantoaxial joints
C3, via the C2–C3 intervertebral disc and paired facet (zygapophysial) joints
c2.note: The dens is held against the anterior arch of the atlas by the transverse ligament of the atlas; if that ligament ruptures or is lax — as in Down syndrome or rheumatoid arthritis — the dens can encroach on the spinal cord (atlantoaxial instability). Bilateral fracture through the C2 pars interarticularis is the "hangman's fracture" (traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis).

c3.function: A typical cervical vertebra: a small body for load plus a large triangular vertebral foramen for the cord, with a transverse foramen conducting the vertebral artery and vein toward the skull.
articulates_with: C2 above, via the C2–C3 disc and facet joints
C4 below, via the C3–C4 disc and facet joints
c3.note: The anterior rami of C3, C4 and C5 form the phrenic nerve — "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive." A complete cord injury above C3 abolishes spontaneous breathing, which is why high cervical fractures are immediately life-threatening. C3 sits at the upper margin of the cervical enlargement, which spans roughly vertebral levels C3–T2 and is widest near C6.

c4.function: Typical cervical vertebra; its small body bears load while its bifid spinous process anchors muscles and its uncinate processes form uncovertebral joints that guide and limit side-to-side motion.
articulates_with: C3 above, via the C3–C4 disc and facet joints
C5 below, via the C4–C5 disc and facet joints
c4.note: A rough clinical level marker: the upper border of the thyroid cartilage and the bifurcation of the common carotid artery are classically placed at about C4, though both vary by roughly a level between individuals.

c5.function: Typical cervical vertebra that carries load through its body while its shallow, obliquely-set facet joints permit the large flexion, extension and rotation range of the mid-to-lower neck.
articulates_with: C4 above, via the C4–C5 disc and facet joints
C6 below, via the C5–C6 disc and facet joints
c5.note: C5–C6 and C6–C7 are the two most frequently herniated cervical discs and together account for the large majority of cases. Map disc to root carefully: a C5–C6 herniation compresses the C6 root (weak wrist extension, diminished brachioradialis reflex, numb thumb), whereas the classic C5 root picture — weak deltoid and biceps with a dulled biceps reflex — usually comes from a C4–C5 herniation.

c6.function: Typical cervical vertebra; its prominent anterior tubercle gives the carotid artery something firm to be compressed against, and its transverse foramen is usually where the vertebral artery begins its climb.
articulates_with: C5 above, via the C5–C6 disc and facet joints
C7 below, via the C6–C7 disc and facet joints
c6.note: The anterior tubercle of C6 is the carotid (Chassaignac) tubercle — palpable between trachea and sternocleidomastoid, and the landmark against which the common carotid can be pressed. The vertebral artery enters the transverse foramen at C6 in roughly 87–92% of people and then ascends through C1; entry at C5 or C7 is the usual variant.

c7.function: The transitional vertebra prominens: its long spinous process is a palpable attachment for the nuchal ligament, trapezius and rhomboid minor, and it hands cervical load on to the thorax.
articulates_with: C6 above, via the C6–C7 disc and facet joints
T1 below, via the C7–T1 disc and facet joints
c7.note: Its transverse foramen usually transmits only small accessory vertebral veins, not the vertebral artery. An extra rib can grow from its transverse process (cervical rib, present in about 1% of people), compressing the brachial plexus and subclavian artery — thoracic outlet syndrome. Its spinous process is usually single rather than bifid, but prevalence of bifidity varies by population: about 0.3% in one white sample, roughly 10% in a southwestern Nigerian CT series.

t1.function: Atypical thoracic vertebra at the cervicothoracic junction: it takes the whole head of rib 1 and begins the rib cage's chain of load transfer while passing neck load into the thorax.
articulates_with: C7 above, via the C7–T1 disc and facet joints
T2 below, via the T1–T2 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 1, on a complete (whole) costal facet, and the head of rib 2, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 1, on its transverse costal facet
t1.note: T1 is atypical because it carries a whole — not half — costal facet: rib 1 articulates with T1 alone. Its spinous process is long and nearly horizontal and can be as prominent as C7's, so counting down from "the bump" at the base of the neck can mislead you by one level.

t2.function: Typical thoracic vertebra: its heart-shaped body carries load while costal facets tie it to two ribs, converting spine and thorax into a single stiff, protective box.
articulates_with: T1 above, via the T1–T2 disc and facet joints
T3 below, via the T2–T3 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 2, on a superior demifacet, and the head of rib 3, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 2, on its transverse costal facet
t2.note: T2 shows the demifacet rule cleanly: the head of a typical rib straddles the intervertebral disc and grips two vertebrae at once — rib 3's head sits on T2's inferior demifacet and T3's superior demifacet. That double grip is part of why the thoracic spine moves so little.

t3.function: Typical thoracic vertebra; its long, downward-sloping spinous process is a muscle lever and its costal facets anchor ribs 3 and 4.
articulates_with: T2 above, via the T2–T3 disc and facet joints
T4 below, via the T3–T4 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 3, on a superior demifacet, and the head of rib 4, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 3, on its transverse costal facet
t3.note: A standard surface landmark: with the arms at the sides, the root (medial end) of the spine of the scapula lies at about the T3 level — one of the quicker ways to start counting thoracic levels on a patient's back.

t4.function: Typical thoracic vertebra; it carries load, anchors ribs 4 and 5, and sits at the mediastinal watershed where the great vessels and the airway divide.
articulates_with: T3 above, via the T3–T4 disc and facet joints
T5 below, via the T4–T5 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 4, on a superior demifacet, and the head of rib 5, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 4, on its transverse costal facet
t4.note: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is classically taught to lie at the T4–T5 disc — the plane of the carina, of the beginning and end of the aortic arch, and of the lower limit of the superior mediastinum. Treat this as a teaching convention rather than a measurement: CT series find the sternal angle at the T4–T5 disc in only about a third of people, and frequently at T5.

t5.function: One of the most typical thoracic vertebrae (T5–T8): a heart-shaped, slightly wedged body that carries load and helps generate the thoracic kyphosis, with demifacets for two ribs.
articulates_with: T4 above, via the T4–T5 disc and facet joints
T6 below, via the T5–T6 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 5, on a superior demifacet, and the head of rib 6, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 5, on its transverse costal facet
t5.note: Mid-thoracic spinous processes slope so steeply downward that the tip of one overlies the vertebra below — they overlap like roof shingles. So the spinous process you palpate does not mark the body of the same-numbered vertebra. The osteopathic "rule of threes" is the classic rough correction for this, but its accuracy has been questioned and it should be treated as an approximation only.

t6.function: Typical thoracic vertebra; body and costal facets transfer thoracic wall load into the column while the long spinous process levers the erector spinae.
articulates_with: T5 above, via the T5–T6 disc and facet joints
T7 below, via the T6–T7 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 6, on a superior demifacet, and the head of rib 7, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 6, on its transverse costal facet
t6.note: Thoracic facet joints lie close to the coronal (frontal) plane, arced as if on a circle centred in the vertebral body — geometry that favours rotation and lateral flexion while limiting flexion and extension. That is the mirror image of the lumbar spine, whose near-sagittal facets allow flexion/extension and block rotation.

t7.function: Typical thoracic vertebra; carries load, anchors ribs 7 and 8, and lies at the transition toward the more mobile lower thorax.
articulates_with: T6 above, via the T6–T7 disc and facet joints
T8 below, via the T7–T8 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 7, on a superior demifacet, and the head of rib 8, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 7, on its transverse costal facet
t7.note: The inferior angle of the scapula is traditionally taught as the T7 landmark, but this is one of the shakiest numbers in surface anatomy: in upright subjects a systematic review and meta-analysis places it nearer the T8 spinous process or upper T9 body, spread across T7–T10. Use it to get close, not to name a level.

t8.function: Typical thoracic vertebra whose body and rib facets carry load; it lies at the level where the inferior vena cava pierces the diaphragm.
articulates_with: T7 above, via the T7–T8 disc and facet joints
T9 below, via the T8–T9 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 8, on a superior demifacet, and the head of rib 9, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 8, on its transverse costal facet
t8.note: The caval hiatus — where the inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm — is at T8. Diaphragm mnemonic: "I ate (T8) ten (T10) eggs at twelve (T12)." Roughly 75% of thoracic disc herniations occur between T8 and T12, with T11–T12 the single most commonly affected level.

t9.function: Lower thoracic vertebra; carries the increasing axial load of the enlarging caudal bodies and anchors rib 9 and, in most people, rib 10.
articulates_with: T8 above, via the T8–T9 disc and facet joints
T10 below, via the T9–T10 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 9, on a superior demifacet, and, in most people, the head of rib 10, on an inferior demifacet
The tubercle of rib 9, on its transverse costal facet
t9.note: T9 is a well-known variant vertebra: in some people it has no inferior demifacet at all, and rib 10 then articulates with T10 alone. From about this level down the spinous processes become progressively shorter and less steeply angled as the column shifts toward lumbar form.

t10.function: Atypical lower thoracic vertebra that usually receives the whole head of rib 10 on a single complete facet; it carries load at the level where the oesophagus leaves the thorax.
articulates_with: T9 above, via the T9–T10 disc and facet joints
T11 below, via the T10–T11 disc and facet joints
The head of rib 10 — typically a single complete costal facet, though a demifacet shared with T9 occurs in some people
The tubercle of rib 10, on its transverse costal facet
t10.note: The oesophageal hiatus is at T10: the oesophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks pass through the muscular part of the diaphragm (formed mainly by the right crus), whose fibres act as a physiological sphincter — which is why hiatus hernia and reflux belong to this level. Below it, T11 and T12 lose their transverse costal facets entirely and take whole costal facets for their floating ribs.

l_rib1.function: The shortest, broadest, flattest and most sharply curved rib; it forms the lateral boundary of the superior thoracic aperture, carries the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus across the top of the chest in the grooves on its upper surface, and anchors the scalene muscles that elevate the whole cage in forced inspiration.
articulates_with: Body of T1 vertebra only (single facet on the head)
1st costal cartilage, which joins the manubrium of the sternum
l_rib1.note: The 1st sternocostal joint is the only one that is a synchondrosis (primary cartilaginous, essentially immobile); joints 2–7 are synovial plane joints. On the rib's upper surface the subclavian vein grooves in front of the scalene tubercle and the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus groove behind it — the anatomy that a cervical rib (present in roughly 0.5–1% of people, and asymptomatic in about 90% of them) can compromise to produce thoracic outlet syndrome.

r_rib1.function: The shortest, broadest, flattest and most sharply curved rib; it forms the lateral boundary of the superior thoracic aperture, carries the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus across the top of the chest in the grooves on its upper surface, and anchors the scalene muscles that elevate the whole cage in forced inspiration.
articulates_with: Body of T1 vertebra only (single facet on the head)
1st costal cartilage, which joins the manubrium of the sternum
r_rib1.note: The 1st sternocostal joint is the only one that is a synchondrosis (primary cartilaginous, essentially immobile); joints 2–7 are synovial plane joints. On the rib's upper surface the subclavian vein grooves in front of the scalene tubercle and the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus groove behind it — the anatomy that a cervical rib (present in roughly 0.5–1% of people, and asymptomatic in about 90% of them) can compromise to produce thoracic outlet syndrome.

l_rib2.function: About twice the length of rib 1 but still atypically thin and flat, it walls the upper thorax beside the lung apex and carries a roughened tuberosity on its superior surface that gives origin to the upper digitations of serratus anterior, the muscle that draws the scapula around the chest wall.
articulates_with: Bodies of T1 and T2 vertebrae plus the T1/T2 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head)
2nd costal cartilage, which meets the sternum at the manubriosternal joint (demifacets on both manubrium and body)
l_rib2.note: The 2nd costal cartilage meets the sternum exactly at the sternal angle (angle of Louis), the palpable transverse ridge that lies at the level of the T4/T5 intervertebral disc — so clinicians find rib 2 by feeling that ridge and count intercostal spaces downward from it, because rib 1 is not palpable beneath the clavicle.

r_rib2.function: About twice the length of rib 1 but still atypically thin and flat, it walls the upper thorax beside the lung apex and carries a roughened tuberosity on its superior surface that gives origin to the upper digitations of serratus anterior, the muscle that draws the scapula around the chest wall.
articulates_with: Bodies of T1 and T2 vertebrae plus the T1/T2 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head)
2nd costal cartilage, which meets the sternum at the manubriosternal joint (demifacets on both manubrium and body)
r_rib2.note: The 2nd costal cartilage meets the sternum exactly at the sternal angle (angle of Louis), the palpable transverse ridge that lies at the level of the T4/T5 intervertebral disc — so clinicians find rib 2 by feeling that ridge and count intercostal spaces downward from it, because rib 1 is not palpable beneath the clavicle.

l_rib3.function: The first of the seven typical ribs (3–9), it encloses the upper thorax and, through its double posterior hinge, rotates in pump-handle fashion to drive the sternum forward and deepen the chest during inspiration.
articulates_with: Bodies of T2 and T3 plus the T2/T3 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head, meeting demifacets on the vertebral bodies)
3rd costal cartilage, then the body of the sternum
l_rib3.note: Ribs 1–3 are short, thick and shielded by the clavicle and scapula, so fracturing them takes considerable force; their fracture is therefore treated as a marker of high-energy trauma and prompts a careful search for injury to the lung apex, brachial plexus or great vessels — though on current evidence an isolated upper-rib fracture with no other signs does not by itself mandate vascular imaging.

r_rib3.function: The first of the seven typical ribs (3–9), it encloses the upper thorax and, through its double posterior hinge, rotates in pump-handle fashion to drive the sternum forward and deepen the chest during inspiration.
articulates_with: Bodies of T2 and T3 plus the T2/T3 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head, meeting demifacets on the vertebral bodies)
3rd costal cartilage, then the body of the sternum

l_rib4.function: A textbook typical rib — head, neck, tubercle, angle, shaft and costal groove — it walls in the mid-thorax, gives purchase to the intercostal muscles that stiffen the chest wall against collapse, and swings on its vertebral hinge to enlarge the thoracic cavity.
articulates_with: Bodies of T3 and T4 plus the T3/T4 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head)
4th costal cartilage, then the body of the sternum
l_rib4.note: Run a finger along the inner aspect of the lower border and you find the costal groove, which shelters the intercostal vein, artery and nerve in that order from top to bottom (VAN) — the reason a chest drain or aspirating needle is passed above the rib below rather than under the rib above. Note the caveat: a collateral branch runs along the superior border of the lower rib, so the safest track is the middle-to-upper part of the intercostal space, not hard against either rib.

r_rib4.function: A textbook typical rib — head, neck, tubercle, angle, shaft and costal groove — it walls in the mid-thorax, gives purchase to the intercostal muscles that stiffen the chest wall against collapse, and swings on its vertebral hinge to enlarge the thoracic cavity.
articulates_with: Bodies of T3 and T4 plus the T3/T4 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head)
4th costal cartilage, then the body of the sternum

Note the caveat: a collateral branch runs along the superior border of the lower rib, so the safest track is the middle-to-upper part of the intercostal space, not hard against either rib.

l_rib5.function: A typical mid-cage rib that overlies the heart and lower lung, transmits the pull of the intercostal muscles, and rotates to expand the thorax in both pump- and bucket-handle directions; its costal cartilage is the uppermost of the three (5, 6, 7) that receive the insertion of rectus abdominis.
articulates_with: Bodies of T4 and T5 plus the T4/T5 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head)
5th costal cartilage, then the body of the sternum
l_rib5.note: On the left this is the cardiac rib: the apex beat is normally felt in the 5th intercostal space (immediately below rib 5) in the midclavicular line, and the 5th intercostal space marks the inferior border of the 'triangle of safety' — bounded in front by the lateral edge of pectoralis major and behind by the anterior edge of latissimus dorsi — into which chest drains are inserted (guidelines commonly cite the 4th or 5th space).

r_rib5.function: A typical mid-cage rib that protects the lower right lung and, in expiration, the dome of the liver — which rises to about this level in the midclavicular line — while transmitting intercostal muscle tension and rotating to expand the thorax during inspiration.
articulates_with: Bodies of T4 and T5 plus the T4/T5 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head)
5th costal cartilage, then the body of the sternum
r_rib5.note: The middle ribs (roughly 4–9) are the longest, thinnest and least shielded by bone or muscle, and are the ones most commonly fractured. Because the liver reaches this high on the right, right-sided middle and lower rib fractures should prompt evaluation for liver injury — in one trauma series about 68% of patients with liver injury had fractures of ribs 5–8 — so a right-sided rib fracture is never assumed to be 'just a rib'.

l_rib6.function: A typical rib of the lower true group; it completes the bony protection of the heart and lung base, participates in both pump- and bucket-handle rotation, and provides the platform on which the abdominal wall begins to grip the thorax.
articulates_with: Bodies of T5 and T6 plus the T5/T6 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head)
6th costal cartilage, then the body of the sternum
7th costal cartilage, via an interchondral joint
l_rib6.note: Rectus abdominis does not end at the ribs by accident: it inserts onto the 5th, 6th and 7th costal cartilages and the xiphoid process, so every sit-up pulls directly on the lower true ribs — this is where abdominal and thoracic mechanics are mechanically coupled.

l_rib7.function: The longest rib and the lowest one to reach the sternum directly; it is the structural keystone of the lower chest, since the chain of false-rib cartilages (10 to 9, 9 to 8, 8 to 7) ultimately delivers the whole costal margin onto its cartilage, and the costal part of the diaphragm arises from the internal surfaces of the lower six ribs and their cartilages, beginning here.
articulates_with: Bodies of T6 and T7 plus the T6/T7 intervertebral disc (two facets on the head)
7th costal cartilage, which meets the sternum low on the body at the xiphisternal junction (and in some people also contacts the xiphoid process)
6th costal cartilage, via an interchondral joint
8th costal cartilage, via an interchondral joint
l_rib7.note: Ribs increase in length from 1 to 7 and then diminish again to 12, so rib 7 is the longest. Beware the common mis-statement that ribs 8, 9 and 10 all attach to the 7th cartilage: only cartilage 8 articulates with cartilage 7 directly — 9 joins 8 and 10 joins 9 — but because the chain terminates on it, the 7th costal cartilage is still the anchor from which the entire costal margin ultimately hangs.

r_rib7.function: The longest rib and the lowest one to reach the sternum directly; it is the structural keystone of the lower chest, since the chain of false-rib cartilages (10 to 9, 9 to 8, 8 to 7) ultimately delivers the whole costal margin onto its cartilage, and the costal part of the diaphragm arises from the internal surfaces of the lower six ribs and their cartilages, beginning here.

frontal.function: Forms the forehead and the roof of both orbits, shielding the frontal lobes and receiving the masticatory loads that travel up the nasomaxillary and zygomaticomaxillary buttresses from the teeth.
frontal.note: You are born with TWO frontal bones separated by the metopic (frontal) suture. Fusion usually begins around 9-12 months and is normally complete by about 6-8 years, but the suture persists into adult life in a minority of people (reported prevalence ranges roughly 1-12% depending on population) — a classic radiology mimic of a skull fracture.

occipital.function: Carries the weight of the head onto the vertebral column through its two occipital condyles and frames the foramen magnum, the doorway through which the brainstem becomes the spinal cord.
occipital.note: It is the only skull bone that articulates with the vertebral column. The atlanto-occipital joint is the "yes" joint — nodding happens here — while most head-shaking "no" rotation happens one level lower at the atlanto-axial joint.

sphenoid.function: Acts as the keystone of the cranial base — a butterfly-shaped central wedge that locks the front and back of the skull together, floors the middle cranial fossa, and cradles the pituitary gland in the sella turcica.
sphenoid.note: The sphenoid contacts every other cranial bone — hence "keystone." Its name is from Greek sphenoeides, "wedge-shaped," and surgeons reach the pituitary by passing through the nose and the air-filled sphenoid sinus (the trans-sphenoidal approach).

l_ethmoid.group: Cranial bones (neurocranium) — left half of the single, unpaired ethmoid
l_ethmoid.function: The left half of the ethmoid forms the left ethmoidal labyrinth: it separates the medial orbit from the nasal cavity via the paper-thin lamina papyracea, carries the left superior and middle nasal conchae that warm and humidify inhaled air, and its cribriform plate transmits the left olfactory nerve fibres into the skull.
l_ethmoid.note: Anatomically the ethmoid is ONE unpaired midline bone — the model splits it into left/right halves for display, so do not count it twice. Its orbital wall, the lamina papyracea ("sheet of paper"), is so thin that a medial-wall fracture lets air pass from the nose into the orbit and eyelid when the patient blows their nose (orbital emphysema).

r_ethmoid.group: Cranial bones (neurocranium) — right half of the single, unpaired ethmoid
r_ethmoid.function: The right half of the ethmoid forms the right ethmoidal labyrinth: it separates the right orbit from the nasal cavity, carries the right superior and middle conchae, and is perforated by the cribriform plate for the right olfactory nerve fibres.
r_ethmoid.note: A fracture of the cribriform plate can tear the meninges and leak cerebrospinal fluid out of the nose (CSF rhinorrhoea) and shear the olfactory nerve fibres, producing anosmia — one reason head-injury patients lose their sense of smell.

l_parietal.function: Forms the left side and roof of the braincase, spreading impact load through its curved shell into the frontal, occipital and temporal bones the way a dome distributes force.
l_parietal.note: Its inner surface is grooved by the middle meningeal artery. At the pterion — where frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid meet — the vault is at its thinnest, and a blow there can rupture the artery beneath and cause an extradural (epidural) haematoma, the classic "lucid interval" head injury.

r_parietal.function: Forms the right side and roof of the braincase, sharing the load-bearing dome of the calvaria with its partner and protecting the parietal lobe beneath.
r_parietal.note: The parietals meet at the sagittal suture; its front end (bregma, where it meets the coronal suture) and back end (lambda, where it meets the lambdoid suture) are the adult remnants of the infant's anterior and posterior fontanelles — the "soft spots" that let the skull deform during birth and expand as the brain grows.

l_temporal.function: Houses and armours the left middle and inner ear inside its dense petrous part, provides the socket (mandibular fossa) for the left temporomandibular joint, and anchors sternocleidomastoid to its mastoid process while its squamous part contributes to the temporal fossa from which temporalis arises.
l_temporal.note: "Petrous" is from Latin petrosus, "stony." The petrous part is the densest, most mineralised bone in the body, which is why the inner ear survives in ancient skeletons and why petrous bone is a prime source of ancient DNA. Its mastoid air cells can be seeded by middle-ear infection, causing mastoiditis.

r_temporal.function: Encases the right hearing and balance apparatus, forms the right jaw socket, and gives passage to the internal carotid artery (carotid canal) and the facial nerve (which exits at the stylomastoid foramen).
r_temporal.note: The facial nerve runs a long, tight bony canal through the temporal bone — which is why temporal bone fractures, and sometimes middle-ear infection, can produce a facial palsy on that side.

mandible.function: The jaw lever: it carries the lower teeth and converts the pull of masseter, temporalis and the pterygoids into biting and grinding force.
articulates_with: Both temporal bones at the temporomandibular joints
mandible.note: The largest and strongest bone of the face, yet it starts life as two halves that fuse at the mandibular symphysis in roughly the first year or two. It is the only large mobile bone of the skull (the three tiny auditory ossicles in each ear also move). The TMJ is unusual: a synovial joint with an articular disc whose surfaces are fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage, and it both hinges and slides.

vomer.function: Forms the posterior-inferior bony nasal septum, bracing the midline partition that splits the nasal airway into two channels.
articulates_with: (6 bones in total, plus the septal cartilage anteriorly)
vomer.note: Its name is Latin for "ploughshare," after its blade-like shape. With the ethmoid's perpendicular plate it forms the bony septum; a deviated septum can involve the vomer, the perpendicular plate, the septal cartilage, or any combination of them.

l_maxilla.function: The left upper jaw: it carries the upper teeth in its alveolar process, floors the orbit, walls the nose, and transmits chewing loads from the teeth up through the facial buttresses into the cranial base.
l_maxilla.note: Each maxilla articulates with nine bones — more than any other facial bone — and is hollowed out by the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus. Because upper molar and premolar roots often project toward that sinus floor, a dental infection can present as sinusitis.

r_maxilla.function: The right upper jaw: it holds the right upper teeth, forms the floor of the right orbit and, with its palatine process, the anterior roughly three-quarters of the hard palate, channelling bite force into the zygomatic and nasomaxillary buttresses.
r_maxilla.note: Cleft palate results from failure of the embryonic palatal shelves (which become the palatine processes of the maxillae and the palatine bones) to fuse; cleft lip arises earlier, when the maxillary and medial nasal prominences fail to merge. Mid-face fractures are graded by the Le Fort classification, which describes three planes along which the maxilla separates from the skull.

l_zygomatic.function: The left cheekbone: a lateral buttress tying the maxilla to the cranium, forming the lateral wall and part of the floor of the orbit, and bridging backwards to the temporal bone to make the zygomatic arch, beneath which the temporalis tendon passes to the mandible.
l_zygomatic.note: From Greek zygon, "yoke" — it yokes the face to the skull. Its four attachments give it the injury pattern known as a zygomaticomaxillary complex (older term: "tripod") fracture, which flattens the cheek and, when the orbital floor is involved, can entrap orbital tissue and cause double vision on upward gaze.

r_zygomatic.function: The right cheekbone: it braces the right orbit laterally and inferiorly and forms the anterior half of the zygomatic arch, giving origin to masseter and passage to the temporalis tendon on its way to the coronoid process.
r_zygomatic.note: Put your fingers on your cheekbone and clench: you can feel the masseter, which originates from the zygomatic arch's lower border and medial surface. Despite feeling solid, the arch is a slender horizontal strut — the zygomatic complex is the second most commonly fractured part of the facial skeleton after the nasal bones.

l_nasal.function: Forms the left half of the bony bridge of the nose, supporting the upper third of the nasal dorsum and anchoring the nasal cartilages that keep the airway open.
l_nasal.note: The nasal bones are the most commonly fractured bones of the facial skeleton — most series put nasal fractures at roughly 40-50% of all facial fractures — because they project forward and are thin.

r_nasal.function: Forms the right half of the bony nasal bridge, giving rigid support to the upper nose and a stable base for the cartilaginous framework below it.
r_nasal.note: Only the upper third of the nose is bone; the rest — the part you can wiggle — is cartilage. A significant nasal-bone fracture is often accompanied by injury to the septum, which is why the septum should always be examined after a broken nose.

l_lacrimal.function: Forms part of the medial wall of the left orbit and, with the frontal process of the maxilla, hollows out the fossa for the lacrimal sac leading into the bony nasolacrimal canal that drains tears toward the nose.
l_lacrimal.note: The smallest and most fragile bone of the face — roughly the size of a little fingernail. Its drainage route is why crying gives you a runny nose: tears pass through the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal cavity.

r_lacrimal.function: Forms part of the medial wall of the right orbit and helps build the lacrimal sac fossa and nasolacrimal canal, the plumbing that carries tears from the eye down into the inferior nasal meatus.
r_lacrimal.note: From Latin lacrima, "tear." When the duct is blocked in infants the tear sac stagnates and the eye waters constantly — congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, a common paediatric presentation that usually resolves on its own in the first year.

l_palatine.function: An L-shaped bone: its horizontal plate completes the posterior part of the hard palate on the left (separating mouth from nose so you can chew and breathe at the same time), while its perpendicular plate forms part of the lateral nasal wall and contributes to the pterygopalatine fossa.
l_palatine.note: The maxillae form the anterior roughly three-quarters of the hard palate and the two palatine horizontal plates form the posterior part; the join between them is the transverse palatine suture. The greater palatine foramen, at the back of the palatine bone, is the target for the dental block that anaesthetises the posterior hard palate.

l_clavicle.function: Acts as a strut that holds the shoulder out away from the ribcage, transmitting force from the arm to the sternum and shielding the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels that pass beneath it.
l_clavicle.note: The clavicle is the first bone in the body to begin ossifying (around the 5th week in utero) and one of the last to finish: the medial epiphysis fuses only in the early-to-mid twenties, which is exactly why forensic examiners use CT of the medial clavicle to estimate the age of adolescents and young adults.

r_clavicle.function: Acts as a strut that holds the shoulder out away from the ribcage, transmitting force from the arm to the sternum and shielding the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels that pass beneath it.
r_clavicle.note: 'Clavicle' is from Latin clavicula, 'little key'; it does rotate on its long axis as the arm is raised, like a key turning. It is conventionally described as the only long bone lying horizontally, and it fractures readily — most often in the middle third after a fall onto the shoulder. (Careful with the common claim that it is 'the most broken bone in the body': that holds for children and newborns, whereas in adults clavicle fractures are only about 2.6–5% of all fractures.)

l_scapula.function: A flat triangular plate that provides the socket (glenoid cavity) for the humeral head and acts as a mobile, muscle-controlled platform that repositions that socket in space as the arm moves.
articulates_with: Head of the humerus (glenohumeral / shoulder joint)
Acromial (lateral) end of the clavicle (acromioclavicular joint)
Posterior ribcage — by muscle only, not a true joint (scapulothoracic)
l_scapula.note: Around seventeen muscles attach to the scapula, and it has no bony joint with the ribcage at all — it glides on the thorax held there by muscle. Because it is so well cushioned, an isolated scapular fracture is uncommon and usually signals high-energy trauma with associated injuries.

r_scapula.function: A flat triangular plate that provides the socket (glenoid cavity) for the humeral head and acts as a mobile, muscle-controlled platform that repositions that socket in space as the arm moves.
articulates_with: Head of the humerus (glenohumeral / shoulder joint)
Acromial (lateral) end of the clavicle (acromioclavicular joint)
Posterior ribcage — by muscle only, not a true joint (scapulothoracic)
r_scapula.note: The glenoid cavity is a shallow saucer far smaller than the humeral head it holds — which is why the glenohumeral joint is the body's most mobile and also its most frequently dislocated joint. The hook-like coracoid process (Greek korakoeides, 'like a crow's beak') anchors pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps brachii.

l_humerus.function: The single long lever of the arm: it transmits load between shoulder and forearm and provides the moment arms (deltoid tuberosity, greater and lesser tubercles) that muscles pull on to swing, lift and rotate the limb.
articulates_with: Glenoid cavity of the scapula (glenohumeral joint)
Head of the radius, via the capitulum (elbow)
Trochlear notch of the ulna, via the trochlea (elbow)
l_humerus.note: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck, so a fracture there — classic in an older patient who falls — can denervate the deltoid and weaken shoulder abduction, with numbness over the 'regimental badge' patch of skin.

r_humerus.function: The single long lever of the arm: it transmits load between shoulder and forearm and provides the moment arms (deltoid tuberosity, greater and lesser tubercles) that muscles pull on to swing, lift and rotate the limb.
articulates_with: Glenoid cavity of the scapula (glenohumeral joint)
Head of the radius, via the capitulum (elbow)
Trochlear notch of the ulna, via the trochlea (elbow)
r_humerus.note: The humerus is a nerve trap: the radial nerve runs in the spiral (radial) groove on the shaft, so a mid-shaft fracture classically causes wrist drop, and the ulnar nerve runs in a groove behind the medial epicondyle — that groove is the 'funny bone', and the tingling you feel is the nerve, not the bone.

l_radius.function: The lateral (thumb-side) forearm bone: it takes most of the axial load from the hand into the forearm and pivots around the ulna to turn the hand palm-up and palm-down.
articulates_with: Radial notch of the ulna (proximal radioulnar joint)
Head of the ulna, at the ulnar notch of the radius (distal radioulnar joint)
l_radius.note: A fall on an outstretched hand most often breaks the distal radius: a Colles' fracture displaces the distal fragment dorsally and gives the classic 'dinner-fork' deformity, while a Smith's fracture (typically a fall onto a flexed wrist) displaces it volarly — the reverse.

r_radius.function: The lateral (thumb-side) forearm bone: it takes most of the axial load from the hand into the forearm and pivots around the ulna to turn the hand palm-up and palm-down.
articulates_with: Radial notch of the ulna (proximal radioulnar joint)
Head of the ulna, at the ulnar notch of the radius (distal radioulnar joint)
r_radius.note: 'Radius' is Latin for the spoke of a wheel, and that is close to what it does: in pronation the radius sweeps across the ulna, crossing over it and carrying the hand with it. Note the division of labour — the ulna forms the true hinge of the elbow; the radius is the rotator.

l_ulna.function: The medial (little-finger-side) forearm bone: the stabiliser, forming the hinge of the elbow with the humeral trochlea and providing the fixed axis about which the radius rotates.
articulates_with: Trochlea of the humerus (elbow joint, via the trochlear notch)
Head of the radius (proximal radioulnar joint, via the radial notch)
Ulnar notch of the radius (distal radioulnar joint)
No direct contact with the carpal bones — it is separated from them by the triangular fibrocartilage complex
l_ulna.note: The olecranon is the bony point you lean on, and it is the insertion of triceps brachii — which is why triceps pull can distract the fragments in an olecranon fracture. A good exam point: the ulna is a forearm bone that does not touch the carpus.

r_ulna.function: The medial (little-finger-side) forearm bone: the stabiliser, forming the hinge of the elbow with the humeral trochlea and providing the fixed axis about which the radius rotates.
articulates_with: Trochlea of the humerus (elbow joint, via the trochlear notch)
Head of the radius (proximal radioulnar joint, via the radial notch)
Ulnar notch of the radius (distal radioulnar joint)
No direct contact with the carpal bones — it is separated from them by the triangular fibrocartilage complex
r_ulna.note: The two forearm bones are coupled by the interosseous membrane and form a closed ring with the two radioulnar joints, so a displaced fracture of one is often paired with a dislocation of the other: a Monteggia injury is a proximal ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation, and a Galeazzi injury is the mirror — a distal radius fracture with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint. Latin ulna means 'elbow/forearm' and is cognate with the old English 'ell' unit of length.

l_scaphoid.function: Spans both carpal rows on the thumb side, acting as the mechanical link that couples the proximal and distal rows and channels load from the thumb column into the radius.
l_scaphoid.note: The scaphoid's blood supply is largely retrograde — the main vessels enter distally — so a fracture at the waist can devascularise the proximal fragment and cause avascular necrosis. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand is managed as a scaphoid fracture even when the first X-ray is normal.

r_scaphoid.function: Spans both carpal rows on the thumb side, acting as the mechanical link that couples the proximal and distal rows and channels load from the thumb column into the radius.
r_scaphoid.note: It is the most commonly fractured of the eight carpal bones. Its name is from Greek skaphos, 'boat'; it was formerly called the navicular of the hand, a term now reserved for the boat-shaped tarsal bone of the foot.

l_lunate.function: Sits at the centre of the proximal row beneath the radius, forming the keystone of the carpal arch through which a large share of axial load passes from hand to forearm.
articulates_with: Hamate — only in a 'type II' lunate, which bears an extra medial facet; this is a common but not universal variant
Triangular fibrocartilage (medially, separating it from the ulna)
l_lunate.note: Kienböck's disease is avascular necrosis of the lunate: the bone gradually collapses, producing a painful, stiffening wrist in a young adult — a reminder that the carpus lives on a precarious blood supply.

r_lunate.function: Sits at the centre of the proximal row beneath the radius, forming the keystone of the carpal arch through which a large share of axial load passes from hand to forearm.
articulates_with: Hamate — only in a 'type II' lunate, which bears an extra medial facet; this is a common but not universal variant
Triangular fibrocartilage (medially, separating it from the ulna)
r_lunate.note: Named from Latin luna for its crescent-moon profile, it is the most commonly dislocated carpal bone. On a lateral X-ray a volar lunate dislocation tips forward into the classic 'spilled teacup' sign.

l_triquetral.function: Forms the ulnar corner of the proximal row, taking load from the little-finger side of the wrist across to the triangular fibrocartilage, and providing the surface on which the pisiform rides.
articulates_with: No direct contact with the ulna — the triangular fibrocartilage disc lies between them
l_triquetral.note: Triangular in shape (Latin triquetrus, 'three-cornered'), it is the second or third most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually as a dorsal cortical chip avulsed in a fall onto an extended, ulnarly deviated wrist.

r_triquetral.function: Forms the ulnar corner of the proximal row, taking load from the little-finger side of the wrist across to the triangular fibrocartilage, and providing the surface on which the pisiform rides.
articulates_with: No direct contact with the ulna — the triangular fibrocartilage disc lies between them
r_triquetral.note: The pisiform, which sits on the palmar face of the triquetrum, is really a sesamoid bone embedded in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris — it articulates with nothing but the triquetrum and takes no part in the wrist joint proper.

l_hip_bone.function: Transfers the weight of the upper body from the sacrum to the left femur, anchors the gluteal, hamstring and adductor muscle masses, and takes the body's weight through the ischial tuberosity when sitting.
articulates_with: Head of the left femur (hip joint)
Right hip bone (at the pubic symphysis)
l_hip_bone.note: It is really three bones — ilium, ischium and pubis — meeting at the Y-shaped triradiate cartilage in the floor of the acetabulum. The triradiate cartilage closes in mid-adolescence (roughly 13-14 years in girls, 15-16 in boys), and the hip bone is not fully ossified until about 20-25 years, when the secondary centres at the iliac crest and ischial tuberosity fuse — so a child's hip bone genuinely shows three separate bones on X-ray. 'Acetabulum' is Latin for 'vinegar cup'.

r_hip_bone.function: Transfers the weight of the upper body from the sacrum to the right femur, anchors the gluteal, hamstring and adductor muscle masses, and takes the body's weight through the ischial tuberosity when sitting.
articulates_with: Head of the right femur (hip joint)
Left hip bone (at the pubic symphysis)
r_hip_bone.note: It is really three bones — ilium, ischium and pubis — meeting at the Y-shaped triradiate cartilage in the floor of the acetabulum. The triradiate cartilage closes in mid-adolescence (roughly 13-14 years in girls, 15-16 in boys), and the hip bone is not fully ossified until about 20-25 years, when the secondary centres at the iliac crest and ischial tuberosity fuse — so a child's hip bone genuinely shows three separate bones on X-ray. 'Acetabulum' is Latin for 'vinegar cup'.

pubic_symphysis.function: Locks the two hip bones together at the front, closing the pelvic ring so load can arch across it, while absorbing shock and allowing a small amount of give during walking.
articulates_with: Right pubic bone (joined by an interpubic fibrocartilaginous disc)
pubic_symphysis.note: A secondary cartilaginous joint (a symphysis), not a fusion, and normally very stiff — on the order of 2 mm of shift and about 1 degree of rotation. Its radiographic gap is normally 4-5 mm; under relaxin in pregnancy it widens physiologically by about 2-3 mm (roughly 4 mm early to ~7 mm at term), and a gap beyond 10 mm is pathological diastasis, not normal loosening. Forensic anthropologists also read the changing face of the symphysis to estimate age at death.

l_femur.function: Acts as the main lever of the left lower limb, carrying body weight from the hip to the knee and giving origin and insertion to the large muscles that drive locomotion.
articulates_with: Left hip bone at the acetabulum (hip joint)
l_femur.note: The longest and strongest bone in the body — and note it does NOT touch the fibula; the fibula stops short of the knee joint. Its head is supplied largely by retrograde branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running back up the neck, so an intracapsular neck-of-femur fracture can cut off the head's blood supply and cause avascular necrosis.

r_femur.function: Acts as the main lever of the right lower limb, carrying body weight from the hip to the knee and giving origin and insertion to the large muscles that drive locomotion.
articulates_with: Right hip bone at the acetabulum (hip joint)
r_femur.note: The longest and strongest bone in the body — and note it does NOT touch the fibula; the fibula stops short of the knee joint. Its head is supplied largely by retrograde branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running back up the neck, so an intracapsular neck-of-femur fracture can cut off the head's blood supply and cause avascular necrosis.

l_patella.function: Sits inside the quadriceps tendon and acts as a pulley, holding the tendon away from the knee's axis so the quadriceps gains a longer moment arm on the left leg, while shielding the front of the joint from direct trauma.
articulates_with: Left femur only — medial and lateral facets against the femoral condyles in the trochlear (patellofemoral) groove
l_patella.note: The largest sesamoid bone in the body, and a classic exam trap: it does NOT articulate with the tibia. It is tethered to the tibial tuberosity by the patellar ligament, but its only joint surface is with the femur. Remove it and extensor power drops substantially (reported losses range from about 30% up to 50%), because the quadriceps loses its moment arm.

r_patella.function: Sits inside the quadriceps tendon and acts as a pulley, holding the tendon away from the knee's axis so the quadriceps gains a longer moment arm on the right leg, while shielding the front of the joint from direct trauma.
articulates_with: Right femur only — medial and lateral facets against the femoral condyles in the trochlear (patellofemoral) groove
r_patella.note: The largest sesamoid bone in the body, and a classic exam trap: it does NOT articulate with the tibia. It is tethered to the tibial tuberosity by the patellar ligament, but its only joint surface is with the femur. Remove it and extensor power drops substantially (reported losses range from about 30% up to 50%), because the quadriceps loses its moment arm.

l_tibia.function: The main weight-bearing bone of the left leg: it receives the load of the femoral condyles on its tibial plateau and delivers most of it down to the talus, and its medial malleolus forms the medial wall of the ankle mortise.
articulates_with: Left fibula (proximal tibiofibular joint and distal tibiofibular syndesmosis)
l_tibia.note: The second-longest bone in the body and the dominant load-bearer of the leg, carrying roughly 85-93% of the axial load transmitted through the leg. Its name is Latin for 'flute' or 'pipe' — ancient pipes were carved from animal shin bones. Its subcutaneous anteromedial surface, the shin, is why tibial shaft fractures so often become open fractures.

r_tibia.function: The main weight-bearing bone of the right leg: it receives the load of the femoral condyles on its tibial plateau and delivers most of it down to the talus, and its medial malleolus forms the medial wall of the ankle mortise.
articulates_with: Right fibula (proximal tibiofibular joint and distal tibiofibular syndesmosis)
r_tibia.note: The second-longest bone in the body and the dominant load-bearer of the leg, carrying roughly 85-93% of the axial load transmitted through the leg. Its name is Latin for 'flute' or 'pipe' — ancient pipes were carved from animal shin bones. Its subcutaneous anteromedial surface, the shin, is why tibial shaft fractures so often become open fractures.

l_fibula.function: Serves mainly as an attachment strut for muscle and as the lateral buttress of the ankle: its lateral malleolus forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise, gripping the talus and limiting eversion. It is not load-free — it transmits on the order of 7% of the axial load with the ankle neutral, rising toward 17% under heavy load.
articulates_with: Left tibia (proximal tibiofibular joint and distal tibiofibular syndesmosis)
Left talus (lateral malleolus, at the ankle joint)
l_fibula.note: Its name is Latin for a 'brooch' or 'clasp pin' — tibia and fibula together resemble an ancient safety pin. Clinically, the common fibular nerve winds around the subcutaneous fibular neck, the most common site of compressive nerve injury in the lower limb; damage there produces foot drop. Note it does not reach the knee joint — it never touches the femur.

r_fibula.function: Serves mainly as an attachment strut for muscle and as the lateral buttress of the ankle: its lateral malleolus forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise, gripping the talus and limiting eversion. It is not load-free — it transmits on the order of 7% of the axial load with the ankle neutral, rising toward 17% under heavy load.
articulates_with: Right tibia (proximal tibiofibular joint and distal tibiofibular syndesmosis)
Right talus (lateral malleolus, at the ankle joint)
r_fibula.note: Its name is Latin for a 'brooch' or 'clasp pin' — tibia and fibula together resemble an ancient safety pin. Clinically, the common fibular nerve winds around the subcutaneous fibular neck, the most common site of compressive nerve injury in the lower limb; damage there produces foot drop. Note it does not reach the knee joint — it never touches the femur.

l_calcaneus.function: The heel bone: it absorbs the impact of heel-strike, transmits body weight from the talus to the ground, and acts as the lever arm for the calf, which pulls on its tuberosity through the Achilles tendon to lift the body at push-off.
l_calcaneus.note: The largest tarsal bone and the most commonly fractured, accounting for about 60% of tarsal fractures. The classic mechanism is a fall from height driving the talus down into it, and because the same axial force travels on up the skeleton, roughly 10-20% of these patients also have a thoracolumbar compression fracture (typically T12-L2). Always image the spine.

The classic mechanism is a fall from height driving the talus down into it, and because the same axial force travels on up the skeleton, roughly 10-20% of these patients also have a thoracolumbar compression fracture (typically T12-L2). l_talus.function: The keystone of the left ankle: the only bone linking leg to foot, it takes the body's weight from the tibia and splits it backwards into the calcaneus and forwards into the arch.
articulates_with: Left tibia and left fibula above (ankle / talocrural joint)
l_talus.note: No muscle or tendon attaches to the talus — it is moved entirely by the bones and ligaments around it — and about 60% of its surface is articular cartilage, leaving very little non-articular surface for vessels to enter. Its blood supply is largely retrograde, running from distal to proximal, so a talar neck fracture is notorious for causing avascular necrosis of the body. 'Talus' is Latin for the ankle bone and also for a die: knucklebones were the original dice.

r_talus.function: The keystone of the right ankle: the only bone linking leg to foot, it takes the body's weight from the tibia and splits it backwards into the calcaneus and forwards into the arch.
articulates_with: Right tibia and right fibula above (ankle / talocrural joint)

Its blood supply is largely retrograde, running from distal to proximal, so a talar neck fracture is notorious for causing avascular necrosis of the body. 'Talus' is Latin for the ankle bone and also for a die: knucklebones were the original dice.

l_navicular.function: The pivot of the left medial longitudinal arch: it passes load forward from the head of the talus into the cuneiforms and provides the principal bony anchor for tibialis posterior, the tendon that actively supports the arch.
articulates_with: Left talus (behind, at the talonavicular joint)
Left medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms (in front, at the cuneonavicular joint)
Left cuboid (laterally — a frequent but variable facet, not present in everyone)
l_navicular.note: Named from Latin navis, 'ship', for the boat-like hollow of its rear surface, which cups the head of the talus. Its tuberosity is the principal insertion of tibialis posterior, and failure of that tendon is the classic cause of adult-acquired flatfoot, with the arch collapsing around this bone.

r_navicular.function: The pivot of the right medial longitudinal arch: it passes load forward from the head of the talus into the cuneiforms and provides the principal bony anchor for tibialis posterior, the tendon that actively supports the arch.
articulates_with: Right talus (behind, at the talonavicular joint)
Right medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms (in front, at the cuneonavicular joint)
Right cuboid (laterally — a frequent but variable facet, not present in everyone)
