Its tuberosity is the principal insertion of tibialis posterior, and failure of that tendon is the classic cause of adult-acquired flatfoot, with the arch collapsing around this bone. Do not confuse it with the scaphoid of the wrist — the old name for the wrist scaphoid was also 'navicular', which is why some legacy texts use one word for two different bones.

groups.title: The Vertebral Column: Cervical, Thoracic, Lumbar, Sacrum, Coccyx and the Intervertebral Discs
groups.teaching: The vertebral column typically contains 33 vertebrae — 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and usually 4 coccygeal (coccygeal number varies from 3 to 5) — and does three jobs at once: it carries axial load down to the pelvis, it houses the spinal cord in a continuous vertebral canal, and, because it is segmented, it still bends. The 24 presacral vertebrae stay mobile; the sacral and coccygeal vertebrae fuse into the sacrum and coccyx. The adult has 23 intervertebral discs: the topmost is C2–C3 and the lowest is L5–S1. Count them carefully — there is no disc between the occiput and C1, and none between C1 and C2, because the atlas has no body of its own (its centrum contributes to the dens of the axis); so the 24 presacral vertebrae do NOT simply have 23 discs between them. Regional shape follows regional job: cervical vertebrae are small and mobile with transverse foramina transmitting the vertebral arteries; thoracic vertebrae carry costal facets and are splinted by the ribs into the stiffest region; lumbar vertebrae are massive with near-sagittal facets that permit flexion and extension while limiting axial rotation; and the sacrum is a fused wedge that transmits load into the two ilia at the sacroiliac joints. Four curves develop in sequence: the thoracic and sacral kyphoses are primary (present in the fetus), while the cervical lordosis emerges as an infant lifts its head and the lumbar lordosis as it stands and walks. Latin os sacrum, traditionally rendered "sacred bone" (a calque of the Greek hieron osteon), names the sacrum; coccyx comes from Greek kokkyx, "cuckoo," whose beak it is said to resemble in profile.

key_counts.label: Total vertebrae
key_counts.note: 7 cervical + 12 thoracic + 5 lumbar + 5 sacral + 3–5 coccygeal (usually 4). Because the sacral and coccygeal elements fuse, the adult articulated column is often counted as 26 separate bones.

key_counts.label: Mobile presacral vertebrae
key_counts.note: 7 + 12 + 5 — the vertebrae that move relative to one another.

key_counts.label: Intervertebral discs
key_counts.note: 6 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar. First disc = C2–C3, last = L5–S1. No disc occiput–C1 or C1–C2, because the atlas has no body.

key_counts.label: Sacral vertebrae
key_counts.note: Fusion is normally complete by the mid-20s to early 30s.

key_counts.label: Coccygeal vertebrae
key_counts.note: The commonest source of disagreement over the 'total vertebrae' figure — 32, 33 and 34 are all normal.

key_counts.label: Rib-bearing vertebrae
key_counts.note: T1 and T10–T12 typically take whole costal facets; T2–T9 use paired demifacets so each rib head straddles a disc and grips two vertebrae.

groups.title: The Thoracic Cage: Ribs, Sternum and Costal Cartilages
groups.teaching: The thoracic cage is the part of the skeleton built to change shape with every breath: twelve pairs of ribs sweep back from the thoracic vertebrae toward the front of the chest, and the seven upper pairs reach the sternum through hyaline costal cartilage — the cartilage is what turns a rigid box into a spring. Posteriorly, a typical rib (3–9) is hinged twice: the head to the bodies of its own vertebra and the one above plus the disc between them (costovertebral joint), and the tubercle to the transverse process of its own vertebra (costotransverse joint). That double hinge fixes an axis of rotation, so ribs do not flap freely — they swing about a set line. The axis lies nearer the transverse plane in the upper ribs, whose "pump-handle" rise lifts the sternum forward and deepens the chest front-to-back, and nearer the sagittal plane in the lower ribs, whose "bucket-handle" swing widens it side-to-side; together they enlarge the thorax in every dimension while the diaphragm descends. Two details worth fixing in memory. First, ribs 1–7 reach the sternum through their own cartilage (true ribs), but ribs 8–10 do not: each joins the cartilage immediately above it by an interchondral joint — 8 to 7, 9 to 8, 10 to 9 — forming the chain of the costal margin (false ribs), while ribs 11–12 end free in the abdominal wall musculature (floating). Second, the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN, top to bottom) run in the costal groove on the internal aspect of the *inferior* border of a rib, best sheltered posteriorly, while a collateral branch runs along the *superior* border of the rib below — which is why needles and chest drains are passed above the rib below rather than hard against the rib above, and why the safest track is the middle-to-upper part of the space, not either rib edge.

key_counts.label: Rib pairs
key_counts.note: Standard in most people, but supernumerary cervical ribs (~0.5–1%) and lumbar ribs do occur, so '12' is the norm, not an invariant.

key_counts.label: True ribs
key_counts.note: Each reaches the sternum through its own costal cartilage. Only the 1st sternocostal joint is a synchondrosis; joints 2–7 are synovial.

key_counts.label: False ribs
key_counts.note: None reaches the sternum. Cartilage 8 joins 7, 9 joins 8, 10 joins 9 — a chain of interchondral joints forming the costal margin.

key_counts.label: Floating ribs
key_counts.note: No anterior attachment; their short cartilages end in abdominal wall muscle. They also lack a costotransverse joint (no articular tubercle).

key_counts.label: Typical ribs
key_counts.note: Head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, shaft and costal groove. Ribs 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12 are atypical; 1, 10, 11 and 12 have single-facet heads.

key_counts.label: Longest rib
key_counts.note: Ribs lengthen from 1 to 7 and shorten again from 7 to 12.

key_counts.label: Sternal angle level
key_counts.note: Anteriorly it is the manubriosternal joint and the level of the 2nd costal cartilage — the starting point for counting ribs, since rib 1 is impalpable under the clavicle.

key_counts.label: Costal groove contents
key_counts.note: VAN from superior to inferior, on the internal aspect of the inferior border; a collateral branch runs along the superior border of the rib below.

groups.title: The Skull: Neurocranium and Facial Skeleton
groups.teaching: The adult skull is conventionally counted as 22 bones: 8 cranial bones enclosing the brain (frontal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid, and paired parietals and temporals) and 14 facial bones (paired maxillae, zygomatics, nasals, lacrimals, palatines and inferior nasal conchae, plus the unpaired vomer and mandible). That count excludes the six auditory ossicles and the hyoid, which are usually tallied separately, so you will also see the figures 28 or 29 — the number depends on the convention, not on the anatomy. Almost all of these bones are locked together by sutures, immobile fibrous joints; the mandible is the only large bone of the skull that moves, hinging and sliding at the paired temporomandibular joints, and the occipital is the only skull bone that meets the vertebral column, at the atlanto-occipital joints. Note that the ethmoid is a single unpaired midline bone even though this model displays it as left and right halves, and that its cribriform plate and paper-thin lamina papyracea make the region between nose, orbit and anterior cranial fossa the most surgically and traumatically hazardous part of the skull.

key_counts.label: Bones in the adult skull
key_counts.note: 8 cranial + 14 facial, the standard convention. Add the 6 auditory ossicles and the hyoid and you get 29; different textbooks state 22, 28 or 29, so always say which convention you are using.

key_counts.label: Cranial bones (neurocranium)
key_counts.note: Frontal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid (all unpaired) plus paired parietals and temporals. The ethmoid is ONE bone despite being modelled here as left/right halves.

key_counts.label: Facial bones (viscerocranium)
key_counts.note: Paired: maxillae, zygomatics, nasals, lacrimals, palatines, inferior nasal conchae (12). Unpaired: vomer and mandible (2). The superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid, not separate bones — only the inferior concha is.

key_counts.label: Bones the sphenoid articulates with
key_counts.note: Frontal, 2 parietals, 2 temporals, occipital, ethmoid, vomer, 2 zygomatics, 2 palatines. It touches every other cranial bone — the basis of the "keystone" description.

key_counts.label: Bones the ethmoid articulates with
key_counts.note: Frontal, sphenoid, 2 nasals, 2 maxillae, 2 lacrimals, 2 palatines, 2 inferior conchae, vomer — the highest count in the skull.

key_counts.label: Bones each maxilla articulates with
key_counts.note: More than any other facial bone: frontal, ethmoid, nasal, zygomatic, lacrimal, palatine, vomer, inferior nasal concha and the opposite maxilla.

key_counts.label: Permanent teeth
key_counts.note: Per quadrant: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars. The count assumes all four third molars are present and erupted, which is often not the case — agenesis of at least one third molar is common.

key_counts.label: Deciduous (baby) teeth
key_counts.note: Per quadrant: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 molars — there are no deciduous premolars; the permanent premolars replace the deciduous molars.

key_counts.label: Hyoid bones
key_counts.note: Usually taught as the only bone that forms no true joint with any other bone: it is slung from the skull, mandible, larynx and sternum by muscles and ligaments. State it as "no bony articulation," not "no attachments" — and note the patella and other sesamoids DO articulate, so they are not counterexamples.

key_counts.label: Auditory ossicles
key_counts.note: Malleus, incus and stapes in each middle ear. They are the smallest bones in the body and they do move — which is why the mandible should be called the only LARGE mobile bone of the skull.

key_counts.label: Bones in the adult body
key_counts.note: A convention, not a fact of nature: it counts the two patellae but excludes other sesamoid bones and any sutural (wormian) bones, which vary between individuals. Real skeletons vary above and below 206.

groups.title: Shoulder Girdle, Arm, Wrist and Hand (Upper Limb)
groups.teaching: The upper limb is built for reach and manipulation rather than weight-bearing, and its skeleton reflects that trade-off at every level. The whole limb is attached to the axial skeleton by a single bony joint — the sternoclavicular joint — while the scapula glides on the back of the ribcage held there by muscle rather than by any true articulation, which is what buys the shoulder its enormous range of motion at the cost of stability. In the forearm, the radius pivots around the relatively fixed ulna to turn the hand palm-up and palm-down (supination/pronation), and the eight carpal bones form an arched mosaic in two rows: an intercalated proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, with the pisiform riding on the triquetrum as a sesamoid) and a distal row rigidly bound to the metacarpals. Motion is shared between the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints, letting the wrist flex, extend and deviate while the arch still transmits grip forces — about 80% of axial load crosses the radiocarpal joint, the rest passing through the triangular fibrocartilage to the ulna. Everything converges on the thumb: a saddle-shaped carpometacarpal joint with the trapezium, plus a first metacarpal that is rotated roughly 90° relative to the others and unattached to its neighbour at its base, is what makes opposition — and a precision grip — possible.

key_counts.label: Bones per upper limb
key_counts.note: 1 clavicle + 1 scapula + 1 humerus + 1 radius + 1 ulna + 8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges. Texts that say 30 are counting only the 'free' limb and excluding the two pectoral girdle bones. Sesamoids other than the pisiform are not counted.

key_counts.label: Bones per hand (wrist to fingertips)
key_counts.note: 8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges. The (usually two) sesamoid bones at the thumb MCP joint are variable and are not part of the 27 — though the pisiform, itself a sesamoid in the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, is counted among the carpals by convention.

key_counts.label: Carpal bones
key_counts.value: 8 per wrist, in two rows of 4
key_counts.note: Proximal row lateral→medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal row lateral→medial: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. Mnemonic: 'Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle.'

key_counts.label: Phalanges per hand
key_counts.note: Three each in fingers 2–5 (proximal, middle, distal) and only two in the thumb — the thumb has no middle phalanx.

key_counts.label: Metacarpals per hand
key_counts.note: Numbered I–V from thumb to little finger. The bases of metacarpals II–V articulate with one another; metacarpal I does not articulate with metacarpal II, which is part of why the thumb column moves independently.

key_counts.label: Bony joints between the upper limb and the axial skeleton
key_counts.note: The sternoclavicular joint. There is no true joint between scapula and ribcage — the 'scapulothoracic joint' is a physiological/muscular articulation only.

key_counts.label: Muscles attaching to the scapula
key_counts.note: The standard teaching count (e.g. TeachMeAnatomy). The scapula is essentially a mobile muscle-attachment plate suspended in soft tissue; exact counts differ slightly between texts depending on how heads and bellies are tallied.

key_counts.label: Share of axial wrist load crossing the radius
key_counts.note: In an ulnar-neutral wrist roughly 80% of axial load passes through the radiocarpal joint and ~20% through the ulnocarpal joint via the triangular fibrocartilage complex.

groups.title: Pelvic girdle and lower limb (hip, thigh, leg, ankle, foot)
groups.teaching: Everything in this region solves one problem: delivering the mass of the upper body down onto two small, mobile platforms without the structure buckling. Load leaves the sacrum, crosses the sacroiliac joints into the hip bones, funnels through the acetabula into the femoral heads, runs down the femur and then overwhelmingly down the tibia — the fibula is primarily a muscle anchor and the lateral buttress of the ankle mortise, though it is not load-free: cadaver studies put its share of axial load at roughly 7% with the ankle neutral, rising toward 17% under heavy or dorsiflexed loading. Below the tibia the load reaches the talus, a bone with no muscle or tendon attached to it, which splits it backwards into the calcaneus and forwards into the arch. Compare this with the upper limb and the trade-off is clear: the shoulder girdle is built for reach and gives up stability, while the pelvic girdle is a closed, load-arching ring that gives up mobility. Two bones here share a dangerous design feature — the femoral head and the talus are both supplied largely by retrograde vessels entering from the far end — which is why an intracapsular femoral neck fracture and a talar neck fracture each threaten avascular necrosis, and why they are treated with more urgency than the break alone would suggest.

key_counts.label: Bones in the pelvic girdle proper
key_counts.note: The two hip bones. The sacrum and coccyx complete the bony pelvis but are counted as axial skeleton, not girdle.

key_counts.label: Bones fused into each hip bone
key_counts.note: Ilium, ischium, pubis — separate in childhood, meeting at the triradiate cartilage, which closes in mid-adolescence.

key_counts.label: Bones in each free lower limb
key_counts.note: Femur, patella, tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges. Both limbs together = 60 of the conventional 206.

key_counts.label: Bones in each foot
key_counts.note: 7 tarsals + 5 metatarsals + 14 phalanges. The two hallucal sesamoids under the first metatarsal head are constant but are NOT included in the standard count.

key_counts.label: Tarsal bones
key_counts.note: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and three cuneiforms. The foot has 7 tarsals; the wrist has 8 carpals — a common mix-up.

key_counts.label: Bones the talus articulates with
key_counts.note: Tibia, fibula, calcaneus, navicular. It is the only bone connecting leg to foot, and no muscle attaches to it.

key_counts.label: Share of leg axial load carried by the fibula
key_counts.note: About 7% with the ankle neutral, rising with heavier loads, dorsiflexion, and laterally shifted load lines. 'The fibula bears no weight' is an overstatement.

tours.title: Why 257, not 206?
tours.subtitle: An honest audit of a number you were told to memorise

steps.title: 206 is a convention, not a law
steps.text: You were taught that an adult skeleton has 206 bones. That is a good number, but it is a count someone agreed on, not a fact of nature. You were not born with it — a newborn has closer to 270 separate bony elements, and many later fuse — and plenty of adults never arrive at it.

steps.title: First, subtract what is not bone: the teeth
steps.text: Thirty-two of the parts you can click here are teeth. Enamel is the hardest tissue in your body — harder than bone — but it is not bone, it does not remodel, and it has never been counted in the 206. A skull that has lost its teeth looks like a skull; a skull that never had them could not eat.

steps.title: Then the discs — 23 of them
steps.text: Between the vertebrae sit 23 fibrocartilage discs, from C2–C3 at the top to L5–S1 at the bottom. Count them carefully: there is no disc above C2, because the atlas has no body of its own. A dry classroom skeleton has lost every one of these, which is exactly why it cannot bend.

steps.title: Cartilage that does a bone's job
steps.text: The costal cartilages carry the upper ribs to the sternum, and the pubic symphysis locks the two hip bones together in front. Neither is bone. The cartilage is the whole point: it is what turns the rib cage from a rigid box into a spring that can change shape with every breath.

steps.title: Now subtract seven bones you cannot click
steps.text: Six of the 206 are the auditory ossicles — malleus, incus and stapes in each middle ear, sealed inside the dense petrous part of the temporal bone, each smaller than a grain of rice. The seventh is the hyoid, slung in the muscles of the throat, the one bone in the body that articulates with no other bone. None of the seven is modelled here.

steps.title: A bone cut in half
steps.text: The ethmoid is a single bone — the delicate honeycomb between your eye sockets that roofs the nasal cavity. This model builds it as a left and a right half, so it costs you two clicks instead of one. That is a modelling decision, not anatomy, and it quietly adds one to the total.

steps.title: And a bone that is simply missing
steps.text: The left little toe here has only two phalanges; the right has three. Its distal phalanx exists in the skeleton's hierarchy but has no geometry, so you cannot click it. That error subtracts one, the split ethmoid adds one, and they cancel — which is exactly why nobody caught either. The ledger closes: 206 − 6 − 1 − 1 + 1 = 199 bones, plus 58 parts that are not bones, is 257.

tours.title: The Axial Skeleton
tours.subtitle: The 80 bones along the midline — the body's mast and its armour

steps.title: The line down the middle
steps.text: Split the skeleton in two and the axial half is everything on the central axis: skull, ossicles, hyoid, vertebral column and rib cage — 80 bones. Its job is not movement but protection and support. Every soft thing you cannot survive without lives inside it.

steps.title: Eight bones make the braincase
steps.text: Frontal, two parietals, two temporals, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid — eight bones fused into one vault by sutures. A suture is a joint that exists to grow, not to move: it lets the skull expand around an enlarging brain in infancy, then locks. Note the ethmoid appears twice here, as left and right halves; that is this model's convention, not anatomy.

steps.title: Fourteen bones hang off the front
steps.text: The face is a scaffold for the special senses and the beginning of the gut: maxillae, zygomatics, nasals, lacrimals, palatines, inferior conchae, vomer and mandible. Every one is locked by sutures except the mandible, the single moving bone of the skull. 8 cranial + 14 facial = 22.

steps.title: Seven bones you will never click
steps.text: Inside each temporal bone, walled in dense petrous bone, sit the malleus, incus and stapes — six bones that exist to lever sound from air into fluid. Below the mandible hangs the hyoid, held only by muscles, touching no other bone. All seven belong to the 80. None is modelled here.

steps.title: The column: 26 bones in the adult
steps.text: Twenty-four mobile vertebrae, the sacrum, the coccyx. It does three jobs at once — carries load to the pelvis, sheathes the spinal cord in a continuous canal, and, because it is segmented rather than solid, still bends.

steps.title: The cage: 25 bones
steps.text: Twelve pairs of ribs plus the sternum. It is the only part of the skeleton designed to change shape rhythmically for as long as you are alive, and it does so around the heart and lungs without ever letting them be crushed.

steps.title: The sum, and why it is worth knowing
steps.text: 22 skull + 6 ossicles + 1 hyoid + 26 column + 25 cage = 80. The other 126 bones are appendicular — the limbs and the girdles that sling them on. The axial skeleton is what you are; the appendicular skeleton is what you do with it.

tours.title: The Vertebral Column
tours.subtitle: Thirty-three become twenty-six: a stack that carries, shields and still bends

steps.title: One column, three impossible jobs
steps.text: The column must carry your whole upper body into the pelvis, wrap the spinal cord in an unbroken bony canal, and still let you tie your shoes. A solid pillar would do the first two and fail the third. Segmenting it — 33 vertebrae, stacked — is the compromise that buys all three.

steps.title: Cervical: small bones, maximum freedom
steps.text: Seven small vertebrae carry the least load and move the most. Each has a transverse foramen — a hole in the side process — through which the vertebral artery climbs to the brain. No other region has these, and they are why a violent neck rotation can tear an artery.

steps.title: Atlas and axis: yes and no
steps.text: C1 is a ring with no body: it cradles the skull on two lateral masses and rocks, which is your "yes". Its missing centrum became the dens of C2 — a vertical peg the atlas and the entire head spin around, which is your "no", and about half of all cervical rotation. Two vertebrae, two axes, two gestures.

steps.title: Thoracic: bought stiffness
steps.text: Twelve vertebrae, each with facets to grip the ribs. Because a typical rib head straddles a disc and grabs two vertebrae at once, the ribs splint the region into the stiffest part of the column. You cannot bend much here — and that is exactly what the heart and lungs need.

steps.title: Lumbar: massive bodies, chosen constraints
steps.text: Five big vertebrae carrying everything above them. Their facet joints sit nearly in the sagittal plane, which permits generous flexion and extension while blocking axial rotation — the mirror image of the thoracic spine. That is why you bend forward from the lower back but twist from the chest.

steps.title: The fusions: 33 becomes 26
steps.text: Five sacral vertebrae fuse into one wedge that drives load out into the two hip bones; three to five coccygeal segments fuse into the coccyx. Fusion is normally complete by the mid-twenties to early thirties. Twenty-four mobile vertebrae plus these two fused blocks is the 26-bone adult column.

steps.title: Twenty-three discs — and why not twenty-four
steps.text: Twenty-four mobile vertebrae ought to have 23 discs between them, and they do — but not where you would guess. The top disc is C2–C3, not C1–C2: the atlas has no body to press against, so there is no disc above C2 and none between skull and atlas. And a disc is not a bone. It is fibrocartilage, and it is a third of the reason this model has 257 parts.

tours.title: The Hand
tours.subtitle: Twenty-seven bones, and why the thumb is not a finger

steps.title: A quarter of your skeleton is in your hands
steps.text: Twenty-seven bones per hand — 54 for the pair, better than a quarter of all 206. Evolution does not spend bone counts on things that do not matter. The hand is expensive because precision is expensive: many small bones mean many small joints, and many joints mean control.

steps.title: The carpus: two rows of four
steps.text: Eight carpals in two rows — scaphoid, lunate, triquetral, pisiform, then trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. The wrist is not one hinge but a shifting mosaic: bending happens a little at every joint between and within the rows, which is why the wrist has such range and yet so rarely dislocates.

steps.title: The scaphoid pays for that mosaic
steps.text: The scaphoid lies across both rows, bridging them — so when you fall on an outstretched hand, it takes the shear. Its blood enters at the far end and runs backwards into it, so a break across its waist can starve the proximal half to death. Snuffbox tenderness with a normal X-ray is still treated as a fracture.

steps.title: The pisiform is a fraud
steps.text: It looks like a carpal and is counted as one, but it is a sesamoid — a bone grown inside the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris — and it merely rests on the front of the triquetral. It touches no other bone and carries no load from hand to forearm. Its job is leverage, not structure.

steps.title: The thumb is a different machine
steps.text: Where the fingers meet flat, gliding joints, the first metacarpal sits on the trapezium in a saddle — concave one way, convex the other. That geometry, plus a 90-degree rotation of the whole thumb ray, is what lets it swing across the palm to meet the fingertips. Opposition is not strength; it is a joint shape.

steps.title: Count the phalanges and the thumb confesses
steps.text: Four fingers with three phalanges each, plus a thumb with only two: 4 × 3 + 2 = 14. The missing middle phalanx is not a defect. A shorter, stiffer thumb is a stronger thumb, and strength is what the opposing member of a pinch grip needs.

tours.title: The Foot
tours.subtitle: Twenty-six bones built from the same parts as the hand, for the opposite purpose

steps.title: Same kit, opposite job
steps.text: Tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges — the foot is built from the hand's parts list, one bone shorter at 26. But the hand must grasp, and the foot must take your entire body weight thousands of times a day and give some of it back. Everything different about the foot follows from that.

steps.title: The talus takes everything and asks for nothing
steps.text: Your whole body weight arrives from the tibia onto the talus. It is pure joint: not one muscle attaches to it. The price of being all cartilage and no muscle is a poor blood supply that runs backwards into the bone — break its neck and the body of the talus can die.

steps.title: The calcaneus is both foundation and lever
steps.text: From the talus, load drops into the calcaneus and out to the ground. But it is also the lever the Achilles tendon hauls on to lift your heel. Fall from a height onto your heels and it shatters — and the same axial force runs straight up your spine, which is why that injury demands a look at the lumbar vertebrae too.

steps.title: Seven tarsals, not eight
steps.text: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms. The hand's eight carpals sit in two tidy mobile rows; these seven are stacked and wedged into a vault. The foot traded a row of mobility for a shape that can hold weight.

steps.title: The arch is a spring, not a vault
steps.text: Follow the medial longitudinal arch: calcaneus, talus, navicular, medial cuneiform, first metatarsal. It flattens as you land, storing energy in ligament and fascia, and recoils to help launch the next step. A stone arch is designed never to move. This one is designed to move and come back.

steps.title: The great toe is the thumb that gave up
steps.text: Like the thumb, the hallux has just two phalanges. But its joint with the first metatarsal is a hinge, not a saddle, and the whole ray is locked into line with the others. It cannot oppose — and in exchange, it is the rigid lever every step pushes off from.

steps.title: And one bone that isn't here
steps.text: Count the left little toe: two phalanges, not three. Its distal phalanx is missing from this model — the right foot has one. There is a true fact hiding behind the error: in a large share of real people the fifth toe's middle and distal phalanges genuinely fuse into a single segment. But not on one side only. This is the model being wrong, and it is worth knowing where your instruments lie to you.

tours.title: The Thoracic Cage
tours.subtitle: True, false and floating — a box that must never stop moving

steps.title: A cage that has to breathe
steps.text: Twelve pairs of ribs and a sternum: 25 bones wrapped around the heart and lungs. Armour is easy; armour that changes volume twelve to twenty times a minute for eighty years is not. Every peculiarity of the ribs is an answer to that problem.

steps.title: Two hinges make an axis
steps.text: A typical rib is hinged twice at the back: its head grips the vertebral bodies and the disc between them, and its tubercle grips the transverse process. Two fixed points define a line — so a rib cannot flap. It must swing about that axis, and the axis is what makes breathing geometric rather than chaotic.

steps.title: True ribs: 1 to 7
steps.text: Each of the first seven reaches the sternum through its own costal cartilage. Their axis lies near the horizontal, so they rise like a pump handle, driving the sternum forward and deepening the chest front to back. The cartilage is what lets a bony ring behave like a spring.

steps.title: False ribs: 8 to 10
steps.text: These never touch the sternum. Rib 8 joins the cartilage of rib 7, rib 9 joins 8, rib 10 joins 9 — a chain that forms the costal margin you can feel under your ribs. Their axis lies nearer the vertical, so they swing out like a bucket handle and widen the chest side to side.

steps.title: Floating ribs: 11 and 12
steps.text: No cartilage forward, no sternum, not even a costotransverse joint at the back — they end free in the muscle of the abdominal wall. Freed from the cage, they stop being armour for the lungs and become a shield lying over the kidneys.

steps.title: Rib 1 is nothing like the others
steps.text: Shortest, broadest, flattest, most sharply curved — it is a horizontal plate forming the rim of the thorax's top opening, and it is hidden under the clavicle so you cannot feel it. Across its upper surface run the subclavian vein, the subclavian artery and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, everything the arm depends on, crossing a single rib.

steps.title: Counting, and the groove that keeps you safe
steps.text: Rib 1 is unfindable, so clinicians feel for the sternal angle — the ridge where rib 2's cartilage meets the sternum — and count down. And under each rib's lower border runs a groove sheltering the vein, artery and nerve, top to bottom. That is why a chest drain goes in over the top of the rib below, and why the safest track is the middle of the space: a collateral branch runs along the lower rib's upper edge too.

quiz.prompt: Find the bone that carries your body weight from the knee down to the ankle — the one that would snap if you landed badly, not the thin one beside it.
quiz.teach: The tibia is the load path; the fibula carries almost none of your weight. The fibula is a muscle anchor and a strut that forms the outer ankle (the lateral malleolus) — which is why a surgeon can harvest a length of fibula for a bone graft and you can still walk.

quiz.prompt: Find the only bone in the skull that moves.
quiz.teach: Every other skull bone is locked to its neighbours by sutures — joints that exist to grow, not to move. The mandible alone has a mobile synovial joint, the TMJ. (Strictly, the three ossicles in each middle ear also move, but they are too small to be modelled here.)

quiz.prompt: Find the bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon in front of the knee — the largest sesamoid in the body.
quiz.teach: A sesamoid is a bone grown inside a tendon. The patella holds the quadriceps tendon away from the knee's axis, lengthening the muscle's lever arm so you can straighten the leg against load. It is the only sesamoid the standard 206 count includes.

quiz.prompt: Find the single strut of bone that connects your entire arm to the rest of your skeleton — break it and the shoulder drops.
quiz.teach: The clavicle is the only bony link between the upper limb and the axial skeleton; everything else is muscle. It props the shoulder out from the chest, and because it is the sole strut it takes the force of any fall onto the shoulder — hence its reputation as one of the most commonly broken bones, especially in children.

quiz.prompt: Find the skull bone pierced by the foramen magnum, the opening through which the spinal cord leaves the head.
quiz.teach: The occipital bone forms the back and base of the braincase. Its two condyles sit either side of the foramen magnum and rock on the atlas (C1) — the joint that lets you nod. Load from the whole skull passes through those two small condyles into the neck.

quiz.prompt: Find the flat bone in the midline of the chest that the upper seven ribs reach through their cartilage.
quiz.teach: Three parts: manubrium, body and xiphoid process. The ridge where the manubrium meets the body is the sternal angle (angle of Louis) — the 2nd costal cartilage joins there, which is why clinicians find rib 2 by feel and count spaces downward from it.

quiz.prompt: Find the vertebra that is a ring with no body of its own — the one the skull sits on.
quiz.teach: The atlas has neither a body nor a true spinous process; its centrum separated in development and became the dens of C2. It is a bony washer that carries the entire skull on two lateral masses. Drive the occipital condyles down into that ring — classically by diving into shallow water — and it bursts: a Jefferson fracture.

quiz.prompt: Find the vertebra that supplies the vertical peg the head pivots around when you shake it "no".
quiz.teach: The dens (odontoid process) of the axis is the pivot; the atlantoaxial joints supply roughly half of all cervical rotation. The transverse ligament pins the dens forward, away from the cord. If that ligament is lax — Down syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis — the dens can encroach on the spinal cord.

quiz.prompt: Find the bone that finally hands your body weight to the ground when you stand.
quiz.teach: The load path is tibia → talus → calcaneus → ground. The calcaneus is the largest tarsal and doubles as the lever the Achilles tendon pulls on to lift you onto your toes. Land on your heels from a height and it is the calcaneus that shatters — which is why such falls also demand a look at the spine, which took the same axial force.

quiz.prompt: Find the bone that receives the entire weight of the body from the tibia — and has not one muscle attached to it.
quiz.teach: The talus is pure joint: it is a weight transfer block wedged in the ankle mortise, and no muscle pulls on it. Its blood supply runs backwards into it from distal to proximal, so a fracture through its neck can cut off the proximal body and kill it — avascular necrosis.

quiz.prompt: Find the forearm bone whose lower end meets the wrist bones directly — the one broken in a Colles' fracture.
quiz.teach: The radius meets the scaphoid and lunate at the radiocarpal joint; the ulna does not touch the carpus at all, being held off by an articular disc. So the radius takes the force of a fall on an outstretched hand, and the distal radius is the most commonly fractured bone in adults.

quiz.prompt: Find the rib that the subclavian artery and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus cross on their way to the arm — a rib you cannot feel, because the collarbone hides it.
quiz.teach: Rib 1 is the shortest, broadest, flattest and most sharply curved rib, and it forms the rim of the thorax's top opening. The subclavian vein grooves in front of the scalene tubercle, the artery and lower trunk behind it. An extra rib growing from C7 (about 1% of people) crowds this same gap — thoracic outlet syndrome.

quiz.prompt: Find the wrist bone that is not a load-bearing carpal at all, but a sesamoid sitting on the surface of another carpal.
quiz.teach: The pisiform is grown inside the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and rests on the front of the triquetral — it articulates with nothing else. Remove it and the wrist still works, because it was never in the path that carries force from hand to forearm.

quiz.prompt: Find the bone most commonly fractured in a fall onto an outstretched hand — tender in the anatomical snuffbox, and often invisible on the first X-ray.
quiz.teach: The scaphoid bridges the two carpal rows, so it takes the shear when the wrist is forced back. Its blood enters at the far end and runs backwards, so a fracture across the waist starves the proximal fragment: avascular necrosis and non-union. A negative first film does not clear it — snuffbox tenderness is treated as a fracture until proven otherwise.

quiz.prompt: Find the carpal bone whose hook forms one wall of the tunnel carrying the ulnar nerve into the hand — commonly broken by the butt of a golf club or bat.
quiz.teach: The hook of the hamate projects into the palm and roofs Guyon's canal, where the ulnar nerve and artery pass. A gripped handle drives straight into it, so hook fractures belong to golf, racquet sports and baseball — and can present as ulnar nerve symptoms rather than pain.

quiz.prompt: Find the carpal bone that gives the thumb its saddle joint — the joint that makes opposition, and human tool use, possible.
quiz.teach: The first metacarpal meets the trapezium at a saddle joint, concave in one axis and convex in the other. That geometry allows the two rotations that let the thumb swing across the palm and meet the fingertips. The freedom costs stability, which is why the thumb base is a classic site of osteoarthritis.

quiz.prompt: Find the skull bone that articulates with every other bone of the braincase and cradles the pituitary gland in its saddle.
quiz.teach: The sphenoid is the keystone of the cranial base — it touches all the other cranial bones and forms much of the middle cranial fossa. The pituitary sits in its sella turcica, which is why surgeons reach the gland through the nose and sphenoid sinus rather than opening the skull.

quiz.prompt: Find the vertebra whose transverse process may grow an extra rib and crowd the nerves and artery heading for the arm.
quiz.teach: A cervical rib arises from C7 in about 1% of people and can compress the brachial plexus and subclavian artery. C7 is also the vertebra prominens — the bump at the base of the neck — and unlike the cervical vertebrae above it, its transverse foramen usually carries only small veins, not the vertebral artery.

quiz.prompt: Find the vertebra at the level where the oesophagus passes through the diaphragm to reach the stomach.
quiz.teach: "I ate (T8) ten (T10) eggs at twelve (T12)" — the inferior vena cava pierces the diaphragm at T8, the oesophagus at T10, the aorta at T12. The muscular fibres around the T10 hiatus act as a physiological sphincter, which is why hiatus hernia and reflux are diseases of this level.

quiz.prompt: Find the structure between the last lumbar vertebra and the sacrum that everyone calls part of the spine — but which is not a bone at all.
quiz.teach: The L5–S1 disc is fibrocartilage: a tough anulus around a gel nucleus, built to be squeezed. It is the lowest of the adult's 23 discs (the first is C2–C3 — there is none above C2, because the atlas has no body). Together with L4–L5 it is the disc most often herniated. Discs are a large part of why this model has 257 parts and not 206 bones.
